topic: Being an Effective Consumer of Food
subject: food-technology

items.title: Why we cure meat with nitrites
items.claim: Sodium nitrite is used in cured meats partly for colour and flavour. What is its main food-safety function?
items.reveal:
C. botulinum produces one of the most lethal toxins known. Nitrites suppress its growth in the anaerobic conditions inside cured meats.

The IARC classified processed meat as Group 1 carcinogenic to humans in 2015 partly due to nitrite and nitrate residues; risks and benefits are now actively traded off in regulation.
items.why: Food additives often combine functional safety roles with health trade-offs.

items.title: Salt iodisation
items.claim: Iodised salt was introduced as a public health measure to address iodine deficiency. In which decade did it first reach mass deployment in the US?
items.reveal:
Iodised salt was introduced commercially in Michigan in 1924, addressing goitre in the 'goitre belt'.

WHO estimates universal salt iodisation has substantially reduced the global prevalence of iodine deficiency disorders since the 1990s.
items.why: Adding a micronutrient to a staple is among the most cost-effective public-health measures recorded.

items.title: Industrial trans fats banned
items.claim: Industrial trans fats from partial hydrogenation were once common in margarine and processed food. Denmark was first to set strict national limits. In which year?
items.reveal_title: Denmark restricted industrial trans fats in 2003
items.reveal:
The US FDA effectively eliminated artificial trans fats by 2018. WHO's REPLACE programme set global elimination targets.

Mortality modelling estimated tens of thousands of cardiovascular deaths prevented in Denmark alone.
items.why: Public-health regulation can change food formulations across an entire economy.
